en.title: MODERN BELARUSIAN BIBLE TRANSLATIONS
en.text:
At the beginning of the 20th century, Wilfred Wiseman, a representative of the British Bible Society, wrote: “Belarusians are one of the first nations to print the Scriptures in their own language. This was in 1517, eight years earlier than the first printed edition in English. One can imagine what Belarusians would be like now if persecution and suppression of the faith at the end of the 16th century had not led the nation to decline. Along with the prohibition and destruction of the Bible, light and hope began to fade.”

Indeed, the decline of the Belarusian language throughout the 18th–19th centuries, as well as the destruction or loss of many earlier editions, effectively left the Belarusian people without the Holy Scripture in their own language. During this time some religious-liturgical books necessary for worship were published, but there was a catastrophic lack of spiritual literature.

Therefore, it is not surprising that alongside the national revival at the beginning of the 20th century, the need for a Bible in Belarusian arose. The first calls for the translation and publication of the Holy Scripture in Belarusian appeared in the press in 1913. The first publications of biblical texts in modern Belarusian were carried out by the pastor from Brest, Łukaš Dzekuc-Malej, who published separate Gospels in Belarusian in Łódź between 1926 and 1928. The British and Foreign Bible Society became interested in a full translation of the Bible into modern Belarusian. In 1931 the New Testament and Psalms in Belarusian were published.

In 1936 the Orthodox Church released its own retelling of the Bible in Belarusian, compiled by Siarhei Paŭlovič, under the title “Sacred History of the New Testament.” In 1939 in Vilnius, “The Four Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles” in the translation of Vincent Hadleŭski, with his commentary, appeared.

In 1954 Piotr Tatarynovič, head of the Belarusian section of Vatican Radio, published in Rome “The Holy Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles,” and in 1974 — “The Letters of the Holy Apostles.”

In Belarus, after attending the Second Vatican Council, Uladzislaŭ Čarniaŭski began translating the Holy Scripture in 1968. The work was completed in the mid-1980s and recognized by the Vatican, but the translation remained in manuscript for a long time.

In 1965 in the USA, the “Belarusian Bible Committee” was founded with the goal of publishing and distributing a Belarusian Bible. In 1970 in New York, “The New Testament of Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” by Janka Stankievič and M. Hitler was published, and in 1973 the full edition “The Holy Bible: Books of the Old and New Testaments” appeared.

Since 1990 the biblical commission of the Belarusian Orthodox Church has been working. In 1991 it published “The Holy Gospel according to Matthew” in Greek, Church Slavonic, Russian, and Belarusian. Other Gospels and Acts followed. In 2017 the New Testament in translation from Greek under the editorship of Archpriest Sergey Hardun was published.

In 2017 the Catholic translation commission prepared and published a complete text of the New Testament.

In 1995 Vasil Siomuha, who had first collaborated with the BOC commission, published his own translation of the New Testament and Psalms. In 2002 a full translation of the Bible, made by Vasil Siomuha in cooperation with the Canadian Global Missionary Service and edited by Yurki Rapiecki, was published.

In 2002 the Bible Society in the Republic of Belarus decided to publish the Bible translated by U. Čarniaŭski. In 2003 the New Testament edition appeared, and in 2012 the full Bible based on Čarniaŭski’s manuscripts was published.

The celebration of the 500th anniversary of the Belarusian Bible and printing in 2017 resulted in mass publication of biblical texts dedicated to this jubilee. Almost 80,000 biblical books in Belarusian appeared at that time.

In 2023 a full Bible translated by Pastor Antoni Bokun was printed. This translation was made from the original languages and has become very popular.

Today Belarusians have three full Bible translations in print and ten translations of the New Testament, not counting translations of individual biblical books. This abundance of translations testifies to the practical need for the Bible in Belarusian so that every Belarusian can read the Word of God in their native language.

en.title: King James Bible
en.text: This edition of the King James Bible was intended for use in church or as a ceremonial Bible for family reading.

en.title: Latin–Polish Bible
en.text: The fourth volume of a bilingual Latin–Polish Bible containing the books of the New Testament. The Latin text is taken from the Vulgate, and the Polish text comes from the late-16th-century translation by Jakub Wujek. The edition is known as the “Kozłowski Bible.” It was created by the efforts of the Belarusian Roman Catholic figure, Archbishop of Mogilev, rector of the Theological Academy in St. Petersburg, theologian, and biblical scholar Szymon Marcin Kozłowski (1819–1899). He was one of the most prolific religious authors of the Russian Empire. Although loyal to imperial authorities, he repeatedly clashed with them due to his unwillingness to introduce additional services in Russian. He popularized the Vulgate translation by Jakub Wujek and emphasized the importance of priests reading the Bible.

en.title: Book of Psalms
en.text: In the 17th–18th centuries, Old Believers fleeing persecution in the Russian Empire arrived in Belarus. Since then, the Vetka district of the Gomel region has become one of the centers of Old Belief. Old Believer culture, “in whose foundation lay the book,” preserved and developed the Old Russian manuscript tradition longer than any other environment. They used the Bible in Church Slavonic, especially valuing editions of the 16th century. It is no coincidence that many books printed by Francysk Skaryna survived specifically among Old Believers. In the 19th century, taking advantage of a decrease in persecution, Old Believers printed biblical texts for their needs.

en.title: Synodal Bible
en.text: In 1816 the Lithuanian–Vilnius branch of the Russian Bible Society began working in Belarus, distributing thousands of copies of the Bible in the early 19th century. Through its efforts, in 1817 the first printed biblical text in Russian — the New Testament — appeared. But in 1824 national Bible translations were banned in the Russian Empire, and a full translation of the Bible into Russian, the so-called Synodal translation, appeared only in 1876. Until then, the Church Slavonic translation made by Cyril and Methodius in the 9th century was used.

en.title: Torah
en.text:
In 1388 the Jews of Brest received a privilege guaranteeing freedom of religion and trade. From this time begins the history of the Jewish community in Belarus. Hebrew manuscripts were present in Belarusian lands from the 14th century. Centers of manuscript creation included Minsk, Grodno, Slutsk, Brest, Mir, and Valozhyn, where in Jewish spiritual schools (yeshivas) the creation of handwritten Torahs continued until the 19th century.

In the 19th century a significant portion of the urban population of Belarus consisted of members of Jewish communities.

The Sefer Torah (“Book of the Law”) is a handwritten scroll on parchment, attached to a wooden roller with carved handles. It was used for weekly public readings in synagogues.

The exhibition features a fragment of a Torah from the village of Trastsianitsa, Kamyenyets District. Created no later than the 19th century, this text of Scripture survived the Holocaust, when the Jewish community of the village was destroyed and the Trastsianitsa Sefer Torah was burned. Only one burned fragment of the end of Genesis and the beginning of Exodus survived.

en.title: “The Gospel According to Luke”
en.text:
The Belarusian biblical tradition almost ceased in the 17th century and revived only in the 20th century during the national awakening.

The Baptist pastor from Brest, Łukaš Dzekuc-Malej, translated the Gospels into modern Belarusian in the early 1920s. He worked on the New Testament together with his wife Serafima and with the support of Anton Łuckievič.

In 1926 the Polish publisher “Kompas” in Łódź released “The Gospel According to Luke.” Between 1926 and 1928 the Gospels of John, Matthew, and Mark also appeared.

In 2021 the National Library of Belarus reprinted the Gospel according to Luke translated by Dzekuc-Malej and Łuckievič.

en.title: New Testament and Psalms
en.text:
Thanks to the support of the British and Foreign Bible Society, in 1931 the entire New Testament and Psalms in modern Belarusian were published.

The New Testament was translated by Łukaš Dzekuc-Malej and the well-known Belarusian political figure Anton Łuckievič. The translation of the Psalms, made by Augusta Rozenberg and edited by Łuckievič, was also included.

To this day, this translation is considered one of the most successful and widespread Belarusian Bible translations. It became the impetus for the publication of 10 later translations of the New Testament and 4 full Bible translations into Belarusian.

en.title: “Sacred History of the New Testament”
en.text: In 1936 the Orthodox Church of Poland prepared a retelling of the Bible for Belarusian schools and self-education. It was compiled by the theologian Siarhei Paŭlovič. In 1964 the book was republished in Cleveland (USA) with funding from Archpriest A. Kryt.

en.title: “The Four Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles”
en.text: In 1930–1932, Father Vincent Hadleŭski prepared and published a paraphrase of the Old and New Testaments and began work on his own translation of the Bible. In 1939 in Vilnius, “The Four Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles” in Hadleŭski’s translation and commentary appeared. The “Four Gospels” were republished in Grodno in 1998.

en.title: New Testament and Psalms
en.text: The New Testament and Psalms translated by Dzekuc-Malej and Łuckievič is the most popular Belarusian translation of biblical texts of the 20th–21st centuries. It has been published six times (1931, 1948, 1985, 1991, 2022, and 2024). The total print run exceeded 60,000 copies.

en.title: Movable type for printing
en.text: Type used for printing biblical books during the Soviet era. Letters were set, as in Gutenberg’s time, in mirrored form to produce a correct readable text.

en.title: “The Gospel According to John”
en.text: A reprint of the Gospel according to John in the translation of Dzekuc-Malej, produced by Evangelical believers in 1973.

en.title: “The Holy Gospel and Acts of the Apostles”
en.text:
In 1954 Father Piotr Tatarynovič continued the work of Vincent Hadleŭski. In Rome “The Holy Gospel and Acts of the Apostles” was published, and in 1974 — “The Letters of the Holy Apostles.”

The translation was based on the Latin–Greek text of the New Testament, scientifically edited and published by Professor August Merk of the Pontifical Biblical Institute. Tatarynovič also used Hadleŭski’s translation and editions in Italian and French.

en.title: “Holy Bible. Books of the Holy Scripture of the Old and New Testaments”
en.text:
In 1965 the Belarusian Bible Committee was founded in the USA to publish and distribute a Belarusian Bible. Its members included M. Hitler (director), J. Stankievič, and T. Sayka. In 1970 “The New Testament” translated by Janka Stankievič was published, and in 1973 a complete Bible translated from Hebrew and Greek in cooperation with Pastor Moses Hitler appeared.

The translation was made from the original languages (Old Testament — Hebrew, New Testament — Greek) and in textual accuracy is comparable to classical translations. At the congress of the American Bible Society, this translation was unanimously approved for publication.

The translation is notable for its abundance of archaic Old Belarusian forms and neologisms. The linguistic peculiarities of Stankievič made this translation difficult to read, as the modern literary language differs significantly from his version.

en.title: “Altar Gospel”
en.text: In 1988 “The Altar Gospel” translated by Metropolitan Mikołaj Macukievič was published, and in 1998 — “The Liturgical Apostolos.”

en.title: “The Gospel According to St. John”
en.text: The Methodist pastor Jan Piatròŭski worked on biblical translations while in emigration. Beginning in 1959 he translated and published individual Old Testament books: “The Book of Ruth,” “The Book of the Prophet Joel,” “The Book of the Prophet Jonah,” “Genesis,” “Ecclesiastes.” In 1991 “The Gospel According to St. John” in his translation was published in Minsk.

en.title: “The Holy Gospel”
en.text: In the 1960s the younger brother of Janka Kupala (Yakub Kolas), Michas Mitskevich, translated the Gospels while in emigration. His translations survived as manuscripts. In 1998 the Gospels of Matthew and Mark were published. The complete translation of the four Gospels was published in 2021. The edition is unique because it is not typeset text but scanned pages of the translator’s handwritten manuscripts.

en.title: New Testament and Psalter
en.text: The famous translator from German, Vasil Siomuha, turned to biblical texts in 1988 and translated the Gospel according to Matthew. In 1990 he published “Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs.” In 1994 and 2008 the Song of Songs was republished, illustrated with engravings by Arlen Kashkurevič. In 1995 Siomuha produced his own translation of the New Testament and Psalms.

en.title: Bible
en.text: In 2002 a full translation of the Bible by Vasil Siomuha from Church Slavonic was published. The work was carried out in cooperation with the Canadian Global Missionary Service and edited by Yurka Rapiecki.

en.title: New Testament
en.text: In 1968, after attending the Second Vatican Council, Father Uladzislaŭ Čarniaŭski from Vishneva began translating the Bible. The work was completed in the mid-1980s and recognized by the Vatican, but remained in manuscript for a long time. Čarniaŭski used the Latin Vulgate, the Russian Synodal translation, the Polish Bibles of Jakub Wujek and the Millennium Bible. In the late 1990s, a group of young believers led by Antoni Bokun began preparing Čarniaŭski’s translation for publication. Over five years a great deal of work was done to edit and compare the text with original-language manuscripts and Bibles in seven languages. This resulted in the publication of Genesis in 1997, the New Testament in 1999, and the Pentateuch in 2002. In 2003 the New Testament edited by the Bible Society was published.

en.title: Bible
en.text:
In 2002 the Bible Society in the Republic of Belarus decided to publish Čarniaŭski’s translation. In 2012 the full Bible based on his manuscripts was printed.

In honor of the 500th anniversary of the Belarusian Bible, the Bible Society republished Čarniaŭski’s translation in 2017.

en.title: New Testament
en.text: In 2014 the New Testament translated by Anatol Klyshka — a Belarusian writer and educator, author of the most popular Belarusian primer (“Bukvar”) — was published. It was translated from ancient Greek and appeared in connection with the 500th anniversary of the Belarusian Bible.

en.title: “New Testament. Book of Proverbs”
en.text: In 2016 Pastor Antoni Bokun published a translation of the New Testament and the Book of Proverbs from the original languages. The edition begins with Francysk Skaryna’s preface to the Bible and is dedicated to the 500th anniversary of the Belarusian Bible.

en.title: “Little Travel Book. Version 2.0”
en.text: In 2017, for the 500th anniversary of the Belarusian Bible, a pocket edition “Little Travel Book. Version 2.0” was published. It contains the Gospel of Mark and the Book of Proverbs in full, as well as selected chapters from the Gospel of Luke and the Psalms translated by Antoni Bokun. The edition also includes Skaryna’s prefaces to the Acts, the Psalms, and the Proverbs.

en.title: “New Testament of Our Lord Jesus Christ”
en.text: In 1989 the Biblical Commission of the Belarusian Orthodox Church held its first meeting regarding translation of Scripture into Belarusian. After publishing the first of the four Gospels — “The Gospel According to Matthew” — in 1991 (in Greek, Church Slavonic, Russian, and Belarusian), the work paused and resumed only in 1995. From 1999 onwards the other Gospels and Acts were published. In 2007 “The Sacred Gospel” appeared — the four Gospels in a form intended for liturgical use. In 2017 the New Testament translated from Greek by the Biblical Commission of the Belarusian Orthodox Church, edited by Archpriest Sergey Hardun, was published.

en.title: New Testament
en.text: In 2017 the celebration of the Belarusian Bible jubilee was supported by the Gideons, who published the New Testament in the translation of the Biblical Commission of the Belarusian Orthodox Church. The edition of 30,000 copies became the largest single print run of a New Testament in the history of the Belarusian Bible.

en.title: New Testament
en.text: The Commission for the Translation of Liturgical Texts and Official Documents of the Roman Catholic Church in Belarus prepared a series of translations of liturgical and biblical texts. Between 2002 and 2005 it produced and published the “Missal Lectionary” — Scripture readings for Mass throughout the year. In 2012 the Commission published the four Gospels under one cover, and in 2017 — the complete New Testament.

en.title: “New Testament for Children and Youth”
en.text: The edition was prepared by the Roman Catholic Church in Belarus to inspire the younger generation to read the Bible. It contains the full text of the New Testament and includes quizzes and interesting facts intended for children and teenagers.

en.title: “New Testament”
en.text: Fiodar Klimchuk, a native of the village of Simanavichy (Drahichyn district), began translating the New Testament into the dialect of his home village in the 1980s. In 2000 the first version of the translation was completed. Over the following years the text was revised and prepared for publication. This unique translation of the New Testament into a Belarusian regional dialect appeared in 2019.

en.title: Bible
en.text: A new translation of the entire Bible into Belarusian from Ancient Hebrew and Ancient Greek appeared in 2023. The work was carried out by pastor Antoni Bokun. The Bible has already undergone three editions (2023, 2024, 2025).

en.title: “Children’s Bible”
en.text: A well-known edition that became the first Bible for an entire generation of young Belarusians. The Children’s Bible impresses with the quality of its illustrations and the adaptation of biblical texts for the very young.

en.title: “My First Bible in Pictures”
en.text: Another children’s edition that was popular in the 1990s. The Bible was printed in Minsk with the support of the International Bible Society.

en.title: Scroll of the Handwritten Book of Proverbs
en.text: The scroll was handwritten in 2018 during the exhibition “Belarus and the Bible” at the National Library of Belarus.

en.title: Codex of Handwritten Books of the New Testament
en.text: The New Testament was handwritten during 2017–2018 in various regions of Belarus. The creation of the codex was dedicated to the 500th anniversary of the Belarusian Bible.
